title: The ENTIRE History of the United States in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of the United States in 10 Minutes (1607–1969)
description:
From a muddy fort at Jamestown to footprints on the Moon, this is the story of the United States from 1607 to 1969 in about ten minutes: the first Americans, the Pilgrims and their beer, slavery, the Revolution, the Louisiana Purchase, the burning of the White House, the Trail of Tears, the Gold Rush, the Civil War, Juneteenth, railroads and immigrants, two world wars and the Moon landing. Every fact is checked.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #ushistory #americanhistory #unitedstates #animatedhistory

beats.say: July 1969. Two American astronauts are walking on the Moon.
Back on Earth, hundreds of millions of people are watching and listening live.
Now rewind about three hundred and sixty years. There's no United States. Just a muddy little fort in Virginia.
Is it always this swampy?
Write home and tell them it's lovely.
So how did a swampy fort become a country that sent people to the Moon? Let's start at the beginning.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of the United States in 10 Minutes
show.sub: From a swampy fort to the Moon, 1607 to 1969

beats.say: First, America didn't start as empty land. People had lived here for more than ten thousand years.
Millions of people, in hundreds of nations, with their own languages, farms, towns and trade routes.
Then Europeans arrived. In 1607, English colonists built Jamestown, in Virginia.
More than half of them died that first winter, from hunger and disease.
The colony survived by growing tobacco, which Europeans paid a fortune for.
In 1619, a ship brought more than twenty Africans to Virginia. They had been kidnapped from Angola and were sold into slavery.
It's the first recorded arrival of enslaved Africans in English North America. Slavery there would last almost two hundred and fifty years.

show.label: Slavery in the colonies and the US
show.sub: from 1619 until it was abolished in 1865

beats.say: In 1620, another ship, the Mayflower, brought the Pilgrims, a group who wanted to worship their own way.
Should we keep looking for the perfect spot?
We can't. We're almost out of beer!
That's real. Their journal says they stopped at Plymouth partly because their food was running low, especially their beer.
About half the Pilgrims died that first winter. The local Wampanoag people helped the rest survive, and in 1621 they shared a harvest feast.
But as more colonists came, they took more and more Native land, often by force. European diseases killed huge numbers of Native people.
By 1732, there were thirteen British colonies along the Atlantic coast.
Britain had just fought an expensive war in North America, and it wanted the colonies to help pay for it.
So Parliament, in London, taxed them: on paper, on glass, on tea.
The colonists were furious. They had no vote in Parliament. Their slogan: no taxation without representation.
In 1773, protesters in Boston dumped 342 chests of British tea into the harbor. That's the Boston Tea Party.
Britain cracked down hard. In 1775, the shooting started.
The colonists picked a Virginia planter and soldier to lead their army: George Washington.
In 1776, Congress, the meeting of colonial leaders, asked Thomas Jefferson, a young Virginian, to write a declaration of independence.
You write it. You write ten times better than I do.
Fine. Somebody pass me a quill.
It said: We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.

show.text: We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.

beats.say: Congress approved it on July 4, 1776. But most delegates actually signed it on August 2.
And those words had a huge exception. Jefferson himself enslaved more than six hundred people during his life.
The war dragged on for years. France joined the American side, and in 1781 the main British army surrendered at Yorktown.
A new country was born. In 1789, George Washington became its first president.
In 1803, Jefferson, now president, bought a giant piece of land from France: the Louisiana Purchase.
He paid fifteen million dollars, about three cents an acre. The country nearly doubled in size overnight.

show.label: The Louisiana Purchase, 1803
show.sub: an acre: $15 million for 828,000 square miles

beats.say: Of course, France was selling land where Native nations already lived. Nobody asked them.
Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark to explore it. Guided partly by Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman, they reached the Pacific in 1805.
In 1812, America went to war with Britain again. And in August 1814, British troops marched into Washington.
The First Lady, Dolley Madison, was still in the White House.
Save the painting of George Washington!
The frame is screwed to the wall!
Then break the frame!
They got the painting out. That night, the British burned the White House. The portrait still hangs there today.
Plot twist: on July 4, 1826, exactly fifty years after the Declaration, Adams and Jefferson both died. Same day, just hours apart.

show.label: Adams and Jefferson both died on

beats.say: Americans kept pushing west, and the government forced Native nations out of the way.
In 1830, Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. In 1838, soldiers forced about sixteen thousand Cherokee people from their homes.
Thousands died on the long march west, through cold, hunger and disease. It's remembered as the Trail of Tears.
Meanwhile, Texas broke away from Mexico in 1836. It was its own country for nearly ten years, then joined the US in 1845.
Then the US fought a war with Mexico and won. In 1848, Mexico had to give up a huge area, including California.
And just days earlier, someone had found gold in California.
By 1849, a flood of fortune hunters, the Forty-Niners, rushed west by wagon and by ship.
Most never got rich. The people selling them shovels and food often did.
Meanwhile, a tall lawyer from Illinois was rising fast: Abraham Lincoln.
Fun fact: he's still the only president with a patent, for a gadget to lift boats over sandbars.
But the country was splitting over slavery. By 1860, nearly four million people were enslaved, most of them in the South.

show.label: Enslaved people in the US, 1860
show.sub: about 1 in 8 people in the country

beats.say: Lincoln was elected in 1860, promising to stop slavery from spreading west. Eleven Southern states broke away and formed the Confederacy.
In 1861, the Civil War began. It became the deadliest war in American history.
At least six hundred and twenty thousand soldiers died. One newer study puts it closer to seven hundred and fifty thousand.

show.label: Civil War deaths, 1861 to 1865
show.sub: soldiers; a 2011 census study estimates about 750,000

beats.say: In 1863, Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in the rebel states free.
About two hundred thousand Black soldiers and sailors fought for the Union.
In April 1865, the main Confederate army surrendered. Days later, Lincoln was assassinated.
In June 1865, Union troops reached Texas and announced that enslaved people there were free. That day, June 19, is now celebrated as Juneteenth.
And in December 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery across the whole country.
After the war, America sped up. In 1869, the first railroad across the continent was finished.
Thousands of Chinese immigrants did much of the hardest work on the western half.
A trip from coast to coast went from months to about a week.
Millions of immigrants arrived, mostly from Europe, sailing past the new Statue of Liberty, a gift from France.
Ellis Island, the immigration station there, processed more than twelve million people between 1892 and 1954.
Out on the Great Plains, it was a brutal time for Native nations, pushed onto reservations after decades of war.
Meanwhile, inventors went wild: electric lights, telephones, and in 1903, the Wright brothers' airplane.

show.place: Near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina · December 1903

beats.say: We flew! You flew!
For twelve whole seconds.
That first flight covered about a hundred and twenty feet. That's shorter than the wings of a jumbo jet.
In 1917, America joined World War One, and helped the Allies win it.
The 1920s roared: cars, jazz, radio, and a stock market that went up, and up, and up.
Then, in 1929, it crashed. In the Great Depression that followed, about one in four workers lost their jobs.
President Franklin Roosevelt launched the New Deal: government programs to put people back to work.
On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the US Navy base at Pearl Harbor, in Hawaii. America entered World War Two.
American factories built planes, tanks and ships at a staggering speed, and millions of women went to work in them.
When the war ended in 1945, the US was one of two superpowers. The other was the Soviet Union.
They never fought each other directly. Instead, they raced: for weapons, for allies, and for space.
In 1957, the Soviets launched the first satellite. Americans panicked, just a little.
At home, Black Americans led the civil rights movement. Leaders like Martin Luther King Jr. helped win new laws against segregation in the 1960s.
And on July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 landed on the Moon.
As he stepped down, Neil Armstrong said: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.

show.text: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
show.who: Neil Armstrong, on the Moon, July 20, 1969

beats.say: Then the crew came home and signed a customs form in Hawaii. Where had they come from? The Moon.
So that's the story so far: from a swampy fort in 1607 to footprints on the Moon, in about three hundred and sixty years.
Next up: the luckiest people in history. See you there.
